To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
hepatic MFs play a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of CLDs, being the main responsible of ECM deposition, and that the origin of these MFs is still controversial.

hepatic MFs are the main cellular source of excess ECM deposition in CLDs and that they represent the most critical cellular crossroad for the integration of incoming signals and for the release of mediators that sustain the fibrogenic and inflammatory response in CLDs.

hepatic myofibsroblasts are the major cellular source of extracellular matrix in chronic liver diseases, and that they are activated from hepatic stelate cells, portal fibroblats and bone marrow-derived cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of hepatic MFs as a major cellular component in the fibrogenesis of CLDs.
the identification of novel molecular and cellular targets that may represent a new therapeutic approach for the treatment of liver fibrosis and cirrhosis.
the identification of the molecular pathways involved in hepatic MFs activation and in their pro-fibrogenesis and pro-angiogenetic responses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the origin, the activation and the functional properties of hepatic MFs represent a key point in understanding the pathogenesis of CLDs, with a major implication in the identification of potential therapeutic targets and in the development of novel and effective strategies in the management of liver diseases.

hepatic MFs represent an important cellular crossroad able not only to integrate and respond to incoming signals, but also to release several mediators which can perpetuate and sustain liver fibrogenesis, inflammation and angiogenesis.

MFs represent the major cell population involved in the progression of CLDs, with a key role in the development of fibrosis, inflammation, angiogenesis and liver carcinogenesis, thus representing an attractive and promising therapeutic target for the treatment of these conditions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

hepatic MFs play a central role in liver fibrogenesis, and their characterization, as well as their origin and functional responses, may provide a novel and promising therapeutic target for the treatment of CLDs.

the hepatic MFs represent a heterogeneous population of cells, with different origins and phenotypes, that are able to integrate the signals coming from all the cell populations involved or present in the microenvironment of a fibrogenic liver.

MFs are the main cellular effectors of liver fibrogenesis, and that their activation, proliferation, migration and ECM deposition are tightly regulated by a complex network of mediators released from the different cell populations involved in the fibrogenetic process.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the MFs are a unique and critical cell population in liver fibrogenesis and that their characterization and study may offer new and promising therapeutic opportunities for the treatment of liver fibrosis.
the MFs are not a single entity, but represent a highly dynamic population of cells that can originate from several sources, and that can express different markers and functions.
hepatic MFs represent the main effector cells of liver fibrogenesis, but their role is not only limited to the deposition of ECM components.
